title: POC scoping: cost modeling with Aldora Systems
next_steps: Send POC statement of work + pricing sheet
Share benchmarking harness and sample prompts
Schedule 1-week baseline benchmark (seeded dataset) w/ SE + infra team
Follow-up on encryption/KMS questions with Security team (Maya to intro)
action_items: Maya Chen - share draft SOW and cost worksheet - 2026-10-04
Ethan Park - provide benchmark harness repo and runbook - 2026-10-02
Priya/Infra - provision test VPC endpoints and temporary creds - 2026-10-05
Samir - share 1k representative sample prompts and expected throughput targets - 2026-10-01
summary: Discovery / POC scoping focused on cost modeling and unit economics for a 6-week POC. Customer provided workload shape (avg prompt 350 tokens, avg response 120 tokens), concurrency targets, and a tight monthly budget. Discussed per-token estimates, batching and caching knobs, expected savings, and benchmark plan. Agreed next steps: share SOW, benchmark harness, and schedule baseline run.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick roll call?
[00:05] Lina Perez: Lina here, hi.
[00:07] Samir Desai: Samir on the line.
[00:09] Priya Kapoor: Priya joining.
[00:11] Diego Ramos: Diego here.
[00:13] Maya Chen: Great. Ethan from infra/SE is with me, he'll dig into the cost knobs. Ethan you wanna intro?
[00:18] Ethan Park: Yup hi all. quick overview: we're looking to scope a 6-week POC to validate latency, cost, and quality for your summarization/assist feature. today we'll run through your workload, success criteria, and then sketch a cost model and benchmark plan.
[00:33] Lina Perez: Sounds good. our goals: reduce time-to-summaries for customer support transcripts, keep latency under 600ms p95 ideally, and keep incremental monthly cost under $12k for the initial deployment.
[00:47] Maya Chen: Got it. can you walk through current traffic shape? tokens, concurrency, that sort of thing.
[00:52] Samir Desai: Sure. current pre-prod: average prompt size about 350 tokens, responses about 120 tokens. about 1,200 requests per hour during peak, so roughly 0.33 rps sustained but bursts to 4-5 rps for short windows. concurrency target for POC we set as 50 concurrent requests to exercise throughput.
[01:17] Priya Kapoor: We also require VPC/private connectivity for the POC, and need to confirm KMS for key management, that's non-negotiable for the security team.
[01:26] Ethan Park: Noted. we can run the POC in dedicated or private mode; both support KMS and VPC. There are unit economics differences I'll go over.
[01:34] Diego Ramos: Quick question: for success criteria, is quality measured by human evals or automated metrics?
[01:38] Maya Chen: We'll include both — human evals from a small panel and automated ROUGE/BLEU-ish scores plus latency and cost thresholds.
[01:45] Ethan Park: Ok jumping into cost modeling - base assumptions: model choice for the POC will be a ~7B open model family (we recommended a 7-13B quantized variant). Our hosted per-token baseline for that profile (on hosted) is approx $0.0009 per input token and $0.0011 per output token at single-request (no batching). that's including runtime and infra amortization.
[02:10] Samir Desai: Those numbers feel a little high relative to our spreadsheet assumptions. can you explain batching impact?
[02:15] Ethan Park: yeah batching can reduce per-token CPU/GPU overhead. with 8-16 request batching we often see 20-40% reduction in effective per-token cost depending on request length and latency SLOs. so if you can accept an extra 20-60ms in tail for batch windows, a realistic per-token can drop to ~ $0.0006 inbound / $0.0008 outbound.
[02:40] Priya Kapoor: how about KV cache/prefix caching? we have lots of repeated prefixes in customer transcripts.
[02:44] Ethan Park: Good point. prefix/KV caching is huge for chatty or repetitive flows. for your workload with repeated prompts, we estimate cache hit rates of 30-45% for prefix reuse, which reduces total generated tokens. in practice that could shave 25-35% off your token bill if prompts are highly repetitive. note transcription: sometimes our logs show "K V cash" spelled weird in earlier notes but it's KV cache.
[03:10] Lina Perez: so together batching + caching could get us below our $12k target?
[03:14] Ethan Park: Possibly. quick back-of-envelope: baseline tokens per request = 470 tokens total. at 1200 rph that's about 564k tokens/hour, ~13.5M tokens/day? Wait, math check — sorry small brain hiccup, let's break it out. 1,200 req/hour * 470 tokens = 564,000 tokens/hour, times 24 = 13,536,000 tokens/day, times 30 = ~406M tokens/month. that seems high — are we sure about 1,200 rph sustained?
[03:46] Samir Desai: Sorry I misspoke earlier, 1,200 per hour is peak hourly not sustained 24/7. sustained average is more like 300 rph, peak 1,200 for short periods.
[03:56] Ethan Park: OK that changes numbers. using 300 rph average: 300 * 470 = 141k tokens/hour, *24 = 3.38M/day, *30 ~101M tokens/month. at $0.0009/input and $0.0011/output combined blended ~ $0.002 per token (very rough) — hmm that doubling is confusing. let's simplify: blended per-token after batching/caching we estimate ~ $0.0009 per token total. at 100M tokens that's $90k/month — still above budget. With aggressive caching and batching we could reduce to $0.0005 per token -> $50k/month. So we need to scope POC to a smaller ingest or prove bigger savings via dedicated capacity.
[04:39] Priya Kapoor: What about dedicated capacity reservation? do we have committed discounts?
[04:42] Maya Chen: Yes for dedicated or reserved pools, we can offer committed usage discounts and different pricing — typically 30-60% lower unit cost depending on commit size and quantization profile. For a POC we can create a short-term reserved instance for the window to show the economics.
[04:58] Diego Ramos: timeline — we have 6 weeks. what's realistic to run these benchmarks and get results we can trust?
[05:03] Ethan Park: Week 1: environment setup (VPC, creds, sample data). Week 2: baseline single-request runs + automated evals. Week 3: batching experiments (batch sizes 4/8/16) + measure latency hit. Week 4: caching/prefix experiments and KV cache tuning. Week 5: scale/concurrency runs and failure/latency SLO tests. Week 6: analysis + exec summary and SOW for rollout.
[05:24] Lina Perez: Sounds reasonable. on success criteria: we'll accept p95 latency <= 600ms for 90% of traffic, end-to-end quality within 8% absolute of our manual summaries (human eval), and monthly projected incremental cost < $15k at 50% production scale.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Good, that's concrete. we'll design benchmarks to map to your production scale and model cost projections.
[05:45] Samir Desai: A couple technical Qs — how do you measure tokenization differences? our prompts have emojis and multi-lingual text which changes token counts.
[05:54] Ethan Park: We'll use the exact tokenizer that the model uses in the harness. we'll warn about tokenization variance; Samir can share a sample dataset and we'll run tokenization stat to produce a per-request token distribution which we'll use in projections.
[06:07] Priya Kapoor: For KMS, we need to see an architecture diagram and confirm that customer keys never leave our account.
[06:13] Maya Chen: We'll include a KMS flow diagram in the security docs, and I will intro you to our security engineering lead to answer any deep questions.
[06:20] Diego Ramos: Are you able to run a canary with dedicated pool and fall back to hosted if capacity spikes?
[06:25] Ethan Park: Yes, smart routing supports fallback. for POC we can emulate and show the failover behavior. note that fallback has cost implications since different pools have different unit economics.
[06:35] Lina Perez: Back to budget — if we commit to a small dedicated reservation for the POC, what are the numbers?
[06:40] Maya Chen: Example: 1 small dedicated GPU pod for the window might bring per-token cost to ~ $0.00025 - $0.00045 depending on quantization and batching. If your effective monthly tokens at 50% production are ~80M, that could be within the $15k target with a modest commit. we'll provide a few scenarios in the cost worksheet.
[07:01] Samir Desai: Quantization — do you support int8 or 4-bit? and what's the expected quality delta?
[07:06] Ethan Park: We support several quantization profiles including int8 and 4-bit dynamic. typical quality delta for summarization tasks on these models is small (<2-4% measured by automated metrics), but we'll validate with human evals in the POC. quant lower memory = more packing = lower unit cost.
[07:22] Priya Kapoor: SLA & logging: we need audit logs per request and token-level cost attribution for chargeback. can you provide that?
[07:29] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns per route and request tracing; we can enable extra retention for the POC. will include retention options in the SOW.
[07:39] Diego Ramos: For the benchmark dataset, we'll share 1k transcripts first. is that enough?
[07:45] Ethan Park: 1k is a good start to get statistical measures. we'll sample for variability. also recommend a set of 100 longer edge-case transcripts to stress tail latency.
[07:55] Samir Desai: Any gotchas on batching with streaming responses? some of our UX expects early partial tokens to show up.
[08:02] Ethan Park: Streaming plus batching is a tradeoff — we support streamed responses but large batching can delay first token; strategies: partial streaming with early flushes, or small batch sizes for streaming routes. we'll test both to find a sweet spot with acceptable first-byte latency.
[08:18] Lina Perez: ok sounds like next steps are clear. can we capture the deliverables?
[08:22] Maya Chen: recap of agreed deliverables: Redwood to send SOW + cost worksheet; SE to share harness and runbook; Aldora to provide sample prompts and provision VPC; schedule baseline run week of Oct 5th.
[08:35] Priya Kapoor: We're also gating on the KMS diagram and SOC2 evidence before we start.
[08:40] Maya Chen: Understood. I'll prioritize security intro.
[08:44] Diego Ramos: timeline: can you send calendar invites for the weekly syncs?
[08:47] Maya Chen: Yes will do right after this.
[08:49] Samir Desai: One last thing — about savings from cache: do you have a recommended cache TTL? our transcripts update occasionally.
[08:55] Ethan Park: Typically prefix caches with TTLs in the 1-12 hour range work; for support transcripts shorter TTLs (30-60m) to avoid stale summaries; we'll test.
[09:05] Maya Chen: Alright thanks everyone. we'll follow up with docs and the SOW.
[09:09] Lina Perez: thanks, talk soon.
[09:11] Meeting ended.
